Howard Zahniser spent eight years writing and rewriting the Wilderness Act. Sixty-six drafts. Eighteen hearings. He lobbied Congress through the Eisenhower and Kennedy administrations, revised the bill every time an industry group demanded a change, and kept going.

He died in May 1964. Four months before Lyndon Johnson signed it into law.

He never saw it pass.

That's the bill that now protects 111.7 million acres. The one the current administration is quietly dismantling around the edges, one roadless area and one mining lease at a time. The one most Americans have never read a word of.

My new piece covers what the Wilderness Act actually is, how it works, who fought for it, and exactly what's being done to it right now.

The Trump administration just rescinded the Roadless Rule — stripping protection from 58.5 million acres of national forest land.

That's not wilderness. That's the buffer around wilderness. The land that feeds the rivers that run through it. The migration corridors. The headwaters.

Leave the wilderness designation technically intact. Destroy everything that makes the wilderness function. That is the strategy, and it's working because most people don't know enough about the law to see what's being taken.

Wilderness areas cover 4.5% of the United States. Strip out Alaska and it's 2.7% of the contiguous 48.

That 2.7% sequesters carbon at roughly the same rate as all other federal lands combined. It produces a disproportionate share of drinking water for Western cities. Counties with wilderness nearby grew in-migration by an average of 8% from 1980 to 2010. Counties without wilderness: zero growth.

The argument against wilderness has always been that it's elitist — land for rich hikers with horses. Frank Church, who shepherded the bill through the Senate, spent his career pointing out that on his own trips into the Sawtooth, he was the only one with a horse. Everyone else had a backpack.

Frank Church was 32 when he got to the Senate, already a cancer survivor who'd been given months to live at 24. When the lead sponsor of the Wilderness Act had a gallbladder attack the night before the 1961 floor debate, Church was asked to take over.

His staff warned him the timber industry, mining industry, and cattlemen would come for him. His own father-in-law called and told him he was out of his mind.

He did it anyway. Took every political hit. Won re-election three more times. Passed the Central Idaho Wilderness Act in his final year in office — 2.4 million acres, still the largest contiguous wilderness in the lower 48.

They named it after him while he was dying. He had four weeks left. When a friend visited at his bedside, Church didn't want to talk about Vietnam or the CIA. He wanted to talk about the wilderness.

If you live in Boise, Salt Lake City, Denver, Portland, Seattle, or Los Angeles and you drink tap water — you drink water that came from wilderness.

You didn't vote on it. You probably don't think about it. But someone put those acres on paper sixty years ago, held the line against every industry lobby that wanted them, and the water kept running clean.

The people who built that system are mostly dead. The people dismantling it are counting on the rest of us not knowing enough to notice.

A 50-49 Senate vote just revoked the mineral withdrawal protecting the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness from sulfide-ore copper mining.

The mine won't sit inside the wilderness. It doesn't have to. The pollution flows in through the watershed.

This is the whole playbook right now: don't touch the designation. Touch everything around it. A wilderness area with its hydrology poisoned and its buffer lands opened to roads and drill rigs isn't a wilderness. It's a line on a map.

The Wilderness Act has been amended and expanded almost every year since 1964. It started at 9.1 million acres across 13 states. It now covers 803 separate areas across 44 states and Puerto Rico.

In sixty years, the system has almost never shrunk. That's not an accident — it's the structural genius of the original law. Zahniser wrote it so that only Congress could designate wilderness, and only Congress could take it away. He'd watched the Forest Service spend decades creating protected areas and then quietly carving them up whenever a road or mine seemed convenient. He removed that discretion from the agencies entirely.

That structure is what's being worked around right now. You can't undo wilderness by executive order. So instead you undo everything else.

There are grizzly bears still living in the lower 48 for exactly one reason: wilderness existed for them to live in.

Not a nature preserve with an entry fee. Not a zoo. Actual untrammeled land, legally protected from roads, motors, logging, and mining, where a bear can move through a landscape without hitting a fence.

There are roughly 1,800 of them left south of Canada. All in or near designated wilderness. The habitat math on this is not complicated.

Aldo Leopold convinced the Forest Service to protect the Gila Wilderness in New Mexico in 1924. First designated wilderness in the world.

Howard Zahniser drafted the federal law in 1956 and spent eight years getting it passed. Died before it happened.

Frank Church carried it through the Senate, took the industry blowback, and kept winning elections in Idaho anyway. Named the biggest wilderness in the lower 48 after him while he was in his final weeks.

Three men. Decades of work. An area larger than California now under the strongest land protection in American law.

My latest piece tells the whole story — who built the Wilderness Act, how it actually functions, and what's being done to it right now while most people aren't watching.

The Fix Our Forests Act is moving through the Senate right now. It shortens environmental review periods, strips judicial oversight, and makes it dramatically easier to log and mine in lands adjacent to designated wilderness.

It's being sold as wildfire prevention. Some of what it does is wildfire prevention. A lot of what it does is make the wilderness system functionally inoperable by clearing out the surrounding landscape that keeps it alive.

The wilderness designation stays. Everything that makes it work gets cut.
